<reason>PRO (B) won by narrowing the debate to a decisive, survivable comparison: cash cannot buy supply that does not exist, while public failure is visible and corrigible. B's rebuttal turn — that CON's own heterogeneity examples (rural parent, thin childcare markets) prove cash chases absent supply rather than solving the gap — inverted CON's best opening argument. The "degraded service vs. zero service" asymmetry in B4 was the strongest single frame, and CON's reply (waiting lists are denial; public systems also cut rural routes first) was real but only partially blunted it, since B's closing answer — that cash failure is invisible and unfixable while public failure generates political pressure — went unanswered. CON's cleverest move, using the welfare-state layering concession against the "rather than" wording of the motion, was met by B's clean ordering response: build the floor first, patch with cash; nobody layers services on top of cash. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 structure. CON's openings and closings were vivid ("expensive wallpaper," "denial with better manners"), but B did more comparative weighing and consistently made the debate easier to decide, while CON's case increasingly reduced to "public services are imperfect," which B successfully reframed as the wrong standard.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.2–B4.4: the survivability asymmetry — a public system's worst day is degraded, corrigible service, while a thin market's worst day is permanent zero with no lever to pull — crystallized the whole debate, and B5 then converted CON's "both systems can deliver zero" concession into the tiebreaker that decided it.</best_rebuttal>
